title: Re'eh: open thy hand (Deuteronomy 15:7–8)
hookLine: don't harden your heart or shut your hand; "thou shalt surely open thy hand"

cards: A man is standing at the light with a cardboard sign. You see him from three cars back. And in the seconds before you reach him, a whole conversation can start up inside.
Do I have cash? Will he spend it well? Is it safe to roll the window down?

The light's about to change anyway. Sometimes, by the time the thinking is done, the moment's gone. The Torah knows that inner conversation, and it names the two body parts where it happens: the heart, and the hand.

teach.h: THE HEART HARDENS, THE HAND CLOSES.
teach.b: In the old Jewish translation: "thou shalt not harden thy heart, nor shut thy hand from thy needy brother; but thou shalt surely open thy hand unto him." Notice the order. The heart hardens first, then the hand closes.
Giving starts inside, before any money moves. And notice the doubling.
Surely open thy hand is, in Hebrew, patoach tiftach: open, you shall open. The rabbis read the double verb as open, and open again. Not once.
The verse goes on: lend him sufficient for his need. His need, not your idea of his need. The word for all of this in Jewish life is today's word, tzedakah.
It's often translated charity, but it shares a root with tzedek, justice, righteousness. Charity sounds like something extra you choose to do when you feel generous.
Tzedakah is closer to what's right, what's owed, part of how a just society works. And how you give matters too.

teach.h: EIGHT LEVELS, A JOB AT THE TOP.
teach.b: The path met Maimonides' eight levels of tzedakah earlier in the year; here's their shape again. Giving grudgingly is the lowest. Giving before you're asked is higher.
Giving so neither side knows the other is higher still. And the highest of all: helping someone with a loan, a partnership or a job, so they won't need to ask again.
A few verses later the Torah says plainly that there will always be poor people in the land. That's not a shrug.
It's the reason the hand must keep opening.

how: Some Jewish homes keep a tzedakah box, called a pushke, and drop coins in before the Sabbath; a tenth of income is a common measure, and Maimonides' eight levels are still taught.

o: a fee paid to join a synagogue
giving to those in need, rooted in justice
a gift given only when you feel generous

s: tzedakah literally means charity, a voluntary kindness
it shares a root with tzedek, justice: closer to what's right and owed.
the verse says the heart hardens before the hand shuts
harden thy heart, then shut thy hand.
Maimonides ranks giving a job above giving a gift
the highest level helps someone so they won't need to ask again.

games.q: you want to give at the highest of Maimonides' eight levels. what do you do?
o: give a large gift with your name on it.
help someone with a loan, a partnership or a job.
games.why: the top level strengthens someone so they won't need to ask again.

practice: Make two fists and feel them, tight and closed; then slowly open them, palms up, resting on your knees. Stay like that, and think of the last time someone asked you for help and you hesitated.
Don't judge the conversation inside you; just notice it, palms open.

wordCard.voice: Tzedakah. Giving to those in need, from tzedek, justice. Not an extra, but part of what's right.

orig.note: Hebrew: righteous giving, from tzedek, justice. often translated charity.
